mcqs.question: In the include/exclude recursion for subsets, what does reaching the base case (end of the input) signify about the current path?
options: That the path is a valid subset only if backtracking hasn't pruned it
That the path is one complete, always-valid subset, regardless of whether it's empty or full
That the path needs a validity check before being recorded
That the path must contain at least one element to be recorded
mcqs.explanation: Unlike combination-sum-style problems where a partial path can become invalid, every leaf of the subsets recursion is automatically a legitimate subset — including the empty one and the full input — because every element has simply been included or excluded, with no constraint to violate. There's no pruning or validity check needed at the base case.

mcqs.question: The start-index version of subset generation calls `result.append(path[:])` at the top of every recursive call, not just when `start` reaches the end. Why?
options: Because otherwise the recursion never terminates
Because it's a performance optimization that has no effect on correctness
Because every prefix built so far, at every depth, is itself a valid subset that needs recording — not only the longest one
Because the start-index version cannot detect when it has reached the end of the input
mcqs.explanation: In this formulation there's no separate "exclude" recursive call — instead, every partial path, at every recursion depth, is a distinct valid subset in its own right, so it has to be recorded the moment the call begins, not just at a designated end state. Skipping this would only capture full-length combinations, missing the empty set, singletons, and every subset in between.

mcqs.question: When skipping duplicates in the sorted start-index loop, why is the condition written as `nums[i] == nums[i-1] and i > start` rather than just `nums[i] == nums[i-1]`?
options: The `i > start` part is only a minor performance tweak and doesn't affect correctness
Without `i > start`, the loop would run past the end of the array
The `i > start` part ensures duplicates are only skipped in the excluded branch, never the included one
Without `i > start`, the very first occurrence of a repeated value at this level would also be skipped, incorrectly pruning a legitimate branch
mcqs.explanation: The first time a value appears at a given `start` position is always a valid new branch to explore; only a repeat of that same value later in the same loop iteration would re-derive a subset the first branch already covers. `i > start` is exactly what protects that first occurrence from being wrongly skipped — dropping it would cut real subsets from the output.

mcqs.question: For input `[1,2,2]`, why does skipping a duplicate value "anywhere it appears in the current path" produce a wrong answer, rather than just a slower one?
options: It silently drops valid subsets like `[2,2]`, which need both physical copies of 2 included together
It causes the recursion to enter an infinite loop
It only affects performance, since the dropped subsets are duplicates anyway
It produces extra, invalid subsets that weren't part of the input
mcqs.explanation: `[2,2]` is a genuinely valid subset of `[1,2,2]` — both distinct physical copies of the value 2 are included together. A path-wide check would see "a 2 is already in the path" and block the second one from ever joining it, silently removing a correct answer rather than just costing extra time.

mcqs.question: Using bitmask iteration over `[1,2,3]`, which subset does `mask = 6` (binary `110`) correspond to?
mcqs.explanation: Binary `110` has bit 1 and bit 2 set (bit 0 is the rightmost), so elements at index 1 and index 2 — values 2 and 3 — are included, giving `[2, 3]`. Reading off which bits are set, from the least significant bit as index 0, is the entire mechanism; no recursion or path list is involved.

mcqs.question: A subset-generation function calls `result.append(path)` instead of `result.append(path[:])`. What does the returned `result` look like once the recursion fully unwinds?
options: A list of 2^n correct, distinct subsets, just built slightly less efficiently
A list where every entry is a reference to the same list object, which has been mutated back down to empty by the time recursion finishes
A list containing only the full-length subset, with all shorter ones missing
A runtime error, since Python does not allow appending a mutable list to another list
mcqs.explanation: Without copying, every append stores a pointer to the one shared `path` list, which keeps getting mutated by later `pop()` calls as the recursion unwinds — so by the end, every entry in `result` points at that same now-empty list. This is the most common bug across backtracking problems: always copy a working list before recording it as an answer.
